days.title: The Cell Cycle & Its Control Points
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the phases of the cell cycle.
  • Identify the three major checkpoints.
  • Explain the importance of checkpoints.
  • Relate cell cycle failure to disease.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell cycle — the series of stages a cell goes through to divide.
  • Interphase — G1, S, G2 phases (90% of cycle).
  • M phase — mitosis + cytokinesis.
  • Checkpoint — a control point that ensures accuracy.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Phases of the Cell Cycle

PhaseWhat Happens
G1Cell grows, carries out normal functions
SDNA replication
G2Further growth; prepares for division
M (mitosis)Nuclear division: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
CytokinesisDivision of cytoplasm

B. Control Points (Checkpoints)

  • G1 checkpoint — checks size, nutrients, DNA damage. If failed, cell exits cycle (G0).
  • G2 checkpoint — confirms DNA replication complete and undamaged.
  • M checkpoint — ensures chromosomes are properly attached to spindle fibers.

C. When Checkpoints Fail

Uncontrolled cell division → cancer. Mutations in checkpoint genes (e.g., p53) allow damaged cells to keep dividing.

💬 Let's Discuss

A cell does not divide at random. It follows a cycle with two big parts: interphase (about 90% of the time) and the mitotic (M) phase. Interphase is not a resting stage — it is the busiest time. In G1 the cell grows, makes proteins and does its normal job. In S it copies (synthesizes) all of its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids. In G2 it makes more organelles and the proteins needed for division. Then in M, the nucleus divides (mitosis) and the cytoplasm divides (cytokinesis).

Like a car passing through checkpoints on a highway, the cell must pass three checkpoints. At the G1 checkpoint it asks: Am I big enough? Are there enough nutrients? Is my DNA undamaged? If the answer is no, the cell may pause or enter G0, a non-dividing state. Most mature neurons and muscle cells stay in G0 permanently. At the G2 checkpoint it checks that DNA was copied completely and correctly. At the M (spindle) checkpoint it makes sure every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers before chromatids are pulled apart.

These checks are run by proteins called cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks), and by guardians such as p53, which can stop the cycle or trigger cell death if DNA is badly damaged.

When checkpoints fail, damaged cells keep dividing and mistakes pile up — the path to cancer. This is why smoking and UV light, which damage DNA, raise cancer risk. Common mistake: thinking DNA is copied during mitosis. It is copied earlier, in S phase.

pairs.why: G1 is the main growth phase where the cell does its usual work.
S stands for synthesis — the DNA is replicated.
In G2 the cell makes proteins and organelles needed for division.
M phase is mitosis plus cytokinesis.
The G1 checkpoint checks size, nutrients and DNA damage before committing to S phase.
The G2 checkpoint confirms DNA was copied completely and correctly.
The M checkpoint makes sure all chromosomes are attached to the spindle.

questions.text: During which phase does DNA replication occur?
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated during S phase of interphase.

questions.text: What happens if the G1 checkpoint fails?
questions.explanation: A cell that does not pass G1 can pause or enter G0, a non-dividing state.

questions.text: Which of the following would result from failure of cell cycle control?
questions.explanation: If checkpoints fail, cells divide without control, which can lead to cancer.

takeaways: The cell cycle has four main stages: G1, S, G2, M.
Interphase is the longest part, occupying ~90% of the cycle.
Failure of checkpoints can lead to cancer.

days.title: Mitosis: Stages & Significance
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the stages of mitosis.
  • Explain what happens to chromosomes in each stage.
  • Identify the significance of mitosis.
  • Explain cytokinesis in plant vs animal cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Mitosis — division producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
  • Chromatid — one half of a duplicated chromosome.
  • Centromere — the point where sister chromatids are joined.
  • Cytokinesis — division of cytoplasm.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Stages of Mitosis (PMAT)

StageWhat Happens
ProphaseChromatin condenses into chromosomes; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle fibers form
MetaphaseChromosomes align at the cell's equator (metaphase plate)
AnaphaseSister chromatids separate; move to opposite poles
TelophaseNuclear envelopes reform; chromosomes decondense; cytokinesis begins

B. Significance of Mitosis

  • Growth
  • Repair and healing
  • Asexual reproduction (in some organisms)
  • Maintains chromosome number (diploid → diploid)

C. Cytokinesis

  • Animal cells: Cleavage furrow pinches cell in two
  • Plant cells: Cell plate forms between the two nuclei

💬 Let's Discuss

Mitosis is how one cell becomes two cells with exactly the same chromosomes. Remember that the DNA was already copied in S phase, so each chromosome enters mitosis as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Mitosis simply separates those copies fairly. A useful memory aid is PMAT.

In prophase, the long chromatin threads coil into short, thick chromosomes that can be seen under a microscope, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and spindle fibers start to grow from the centrosomes. In metaphase, the chromosomes line up single-file along the middle of the cell (the metaphase plate) — M for middle. In anaphase, the centromeres split and the sister chromatids are pulled toward opposite poles — A for apart. In telophase, the chromosomes uncoil and a nuclear envelope forms around each set — T for two nuclei.

Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. In animal cells, a ring of actin pinches the membrane inward to form a cleavage furrow, like tightening a drawstring bag. Plant cells cannot pinch because of their rigid wall, so vesicles from the Golgi build a cell plate across the middle that becomes a new wall.

Why is mitosis important? It allows growth (one zygote becomes trillions of cells), repair (healing wounds, replacing skin and blood cells) and asexual reproduction (yeast budding, new plants from cuttings). Common mistake: saying chromosomes are "copied" in anaphase. They are only separated there; copying happened in S phase.

pairs.why: In prophase chromosomes condense and the spindle starts forming.
In metaphase chromosomes line up at the middle (equator).
In anaphase sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles.
In telophase nuclear envelopes form around the two sets.
Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm into two cells.
Mitosis makes identical cells for growth and tissue repair.

questions.explanation: Chromosomes align at the equator in metaphase.

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces identical cells for growth and repair; diversity comes from meiosis.

choices.label: There is no difference at all
Animal: cleavage furrow; plant: cell plate
Plant: cleavage furrow; animal: cell plate

takeaways: Mitosis has four stages: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (PMAT).
It produces two genetically identical diploid cells.
Mitosis is for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.
Cytokinesis differs: cleavage furrow (animal) vs cell plate (plant).

days.title: Meiosis: Stages & Crossing Over
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the stages of meiosis.
  • Explain crossing over and recombination.
  • Differentiate mitosis from meiosis.
  • Explain how meiosis generates genetic diversity.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Meiosis — reduction division producing four haploid cells.
  • Homologous chromosomes — pairs of chromosomes (one from each parent).
  • Crossing over — exchange of segments between homologs.
  • Chiasma — the point of crossing over.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Two Rounds of Division

StageKey Event
Prophase IHomologs pair (synapsis); crossing over occurs
Metaphase IHomolog pairs line up at equator
Anaphase IHomologs separate (not sister chromatids)
Telophase ITwo haploid cells formed
Meiosis IISister chromatids separate — like mitosis

B. Crossing Over

During Prophase I, homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata. This creates new allele combinations, generating genetic diversity.

C. Mitosis vs Meiosis

AspectMitosisMeiosis
PurposeGrowth, repairGametes
Divisions12
Daughter cells2 (diploid)4 (haploid)
Genetic diversityNoYes
Crossing overNoYes

💬 Let's Discuss

If body cells used mitosis to make eggs and sperm, each gamete would have 46 chromosomes and the baby would have 92 — and the number would double every generation. Meiosis solves this. It is a reduction division: one diploid cell (2n = 46 in humans) divides twice to make four haploid cells (n = 23), each genetically different.

Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes — the matching pair you received, one from your mother and one from your father. In prophase I, homologs pair up closely (synapsis) and swap segments at points called chiasmata. This is crossing over, and it creates chromosomes with new combinations of alleles. In metaphase I, the pairs line up at the equator, and each pair's orientation is random — this is independent assortment. In anaphase I, homologs move to opposite poles, while sister chromatids stay together. Telophase I gives two haploid cells.

Meiosis II works like mitosis: the sister chromatids finally separate, giving four haploid cells in total.

Crossing over plus independent assortment (over 8 million combinations from 23 pairs alone) plus random fertilization explain why siblings with the same parents look different. Genetic variety helps a population survive changing environments.

Compare: mitosis = 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells, for growth and repair; meiosis = 2 divisions, 4 unique haploid cells, for gametes. Common mistake: thinking homologous chromosomes are the same as sister chromatids. Sisters are identical copies; homologs carry the same genes but may have different alleles.

pairs.why: Crossing over happens in prophase I when homologs pair up.
In metaphase I homologous pairs, not single chromosomes, line up at the equator.
In anaphase I the homologs separate; sister chromatids stay joined.
Telophase I ends with two haploid cells.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis.
Crossing over is the exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes.
A chiasma is the visible X-shaped point where crossing over happened.

scenarios.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (2n → n).

questions.explanation: Crossing over takes place in prophase I.

questions.explanation: Two divisions (meiosis I and II) give four daughter cells.

questions.explanation: Swapping segments between homologs creates new allele combinations, increasing diversity.

Crossing over in Prophase I generates genetic diversity.
Homologs separate in Anaphase I; sister chromatids in Anaphase II.
Mitosis produces identical cells; meiosis produces diverse gametes.

days.title: Applications & Cell Cycle Disorders
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain applications of mitosis and meiosis.
  • Identify disorders caused by cell cycle malfunction.
  • Describe how cancer develops.
  • Explain nondisjunction and its effects.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nondisjunction — failure of chromosomes to separate properly.
  • Aneuploidy — abnormal chromosome number.
  • Oncogene — gene that promotes cancer.
  • Tumor suppressor gene — gene that prevents cancer (e.g., p53).

📚 Lesson Content

A. Applications of Mitosis

  • Wound healing and tissue repair
  • Asexual reproduction in plants (cuttings, grafting)
  • Cloning
  • Cancer research (studying uncontrolled division)

B. Applications of Meiosis

  • Gamete production (sperm/egg)
  • Genetic diversity in offspring
  • Selective breeding
  • Understanding genetic disorders

C. Cell Cycle Disorders

DisorderCause
CancerUncontrolled cell division
Down syndromeTrisomy 21 (nondisjunction)
Turner syndromeMonosomy X
Klinefelter syndromeXXY

💬 Let's Discuss

Because cell division is everywhere in life, errors in it are behind several important health conditions — and understanding it also gives us tools for medicine and agriculture.

Cancer is mitosis out of control. Normally, proto-oncogenes act like a car's gas pedal (they promote division) and tumor suppressor genes act like the brakes. The best-known brake is p53, which stops the cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger cell suicide (apoptosis). If mutations jam the gas pedal or cut the brakes, cells divide again and again, forming a tumor. When tumor cells invade other tissues, the cancer is malignant and can spread (metastasize). Many chemotherapy drugs work by blocking the spindle or DNA copying in rapidly dividing cells — which is also why hair cells and the lining of the gut are affected, causing hair loss and nausea.

Meiosis errors produce cells with the wrong number of chromosomes. In nondisjunction, homologs (in meiosis I) or chromatids (in meiosis II) fail to separate, so one gamete gets an extra chromosome and another gets one fewer. If such a gamete is fertilized: an extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome (trisomy 21); one X with no second sex chromosome causes Turner syndrome (45,X); XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome. The risk of nondisjunction increases with maternal age.

On the useful side, mitosis lets gardeners grow new plants from cuttings and lets scientists grow tissues in the lab. Doctors use a karyotype — a photo of chromosomes arranged in pairs — to detect these conditions. Common mistake: thinking all tumors are cancer. Benign tumors do not invade or spread.

pairs.why: Cancer cells keep dividing because their cell-cycle controls are broken.
Down syndrome results from three copies of chromosome 21.
Turner syndrome results from a single X chromosome (45,X).
Klinefelter syndrome results from an extra X in a male (47,XXY).
p53 is a tumor suppressor that stops division when DNA is damaged.
Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate.

scenarios.explanation: Healing replaces lost cells through mitosis.

scenarios.explanation: Sperm are gametes produced by meiosis.

scenarios.explanation: A new plant from a cutting grows by mitosis.

scenarios.text: Genetic diversity is generated in offspring.
scenarios.explanation: Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis create diversity.

scenarios.explanation: A tumor forms when mitosis continues without control.

scenarios.text: A zygote has an extra chromosome 21.
scenarios.explanation: An extra chromosome 21 comes from nondisjunction during meiosis.

questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 — three copies of chromosome 21 — causes Down syndrome.

questions.text: Which application is specific to mitosis?
questions.explanation: Wound healing needs identical replacement cells, made by mitosis.

questions.text: What is a tumor suppressor gene?

choices.label: A gene that causes cancer to spread
A gene that stops uncontrolled division
A gene found only in prokaryotes
A gene that codes for ribosomes

questions.explanation: Tumor suppressor genes such as p53 act as brakes that stop uncontrolled division.

takeaways: Mitosis is applied in healing, asexual reproduction, and cloning.
Meiosis is applied in gamete production, diversity, and breeding.
Nondisjunction leads to aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome).
Cancer results from mutations in cell cycle control genes.
